A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPECTRE research work. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable matching of retained, revised, and added content.

before.justification: v1 reports original SPECTRE results for biomarker classification, semantic segmentation, and text-to-image retrieval, together with optimization and crop-size ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds TotalSegmentator evaluations, decoder and small-lesion experiments, and retrieval robustness analyses.

M1.justification: C.2.7 adds linear-head and UNETR-style segmentation adaptations of the pretrained encoder, changing the decoding procedure in these experiments. The SPECTRE backbone, two-stage pretraining objectives, and default SEoMT procedure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds broader anatomical segmentation on TotalSegmentator benchmarks covering 104, 117, and 20 structures, plus evaluations focused on lesions below 10 mm, corrupted reports, and native voxel spacing. AMOS is removed from quantitative segmentation benchmarking because it was used for pretraining; its pretraining use and Figure 6 examples remain.

E2.justification: Table 9 adds segmentation comparisons with SuPreM, CT-FM, Merlin, and SAM-Med3D with one or ten clicks. SuPreM, CT-FM, and Merlin previously appeared in other task comparisons, but these segmentation comparisons are new. C.3.1 also adds MedSigLIP to CT-RATE retrieval evaluation.

E3.justification: Table 10 introduces retrained fold-0 decoder comparisons at matched 37.5k and 75k training steps, with a separately identified 250k-step nnU-Net reference, and adds NSD and small-lesion detection metrics. C.3 adds corruption procedures, a 500-token report-length threshold, and native-spacing evaluation. These are additional protocols; the retained headline experiments keep their previous settings.

E4.justification: New analyses test how decoder choice and training budget affect segmentation and tiny-lesion sensitivity, and how retrieval responds to voxel spacing, token versus span dropout, and report length. The existing optimizer, deep-supervision, initialization, and crop-size ablations are retained as Table 8, formerly Table 7.

E5.justification: The existing 95% confidence intervals across cross-validation folds in Figure 3 are unchanged. New Figure 8 contains shaded bands, but its caption and accompanying text do not define their statistical meaning or report runs or seeds. Whether these introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice cannot be established reliably.

E6.justification: Table 9 adds SPECTRE Dice scores of 87.34, 88.85, and 87.29 on its three TotalSegmentator benchmarks. New Table 10 reports, for example, 1.53% versus 11.12% tiny-lesion detection for SEoMT versus UNETR at 37.5k steps. Retrieval robustness and MedSigLIP results are also added. Retained headline scores and the original ablation values are unchanged; the AMOS Dice result of 87.55 is removed.

T1.justification: The mathematical architecture and loss formulations in Sections 3–4, including all 20 numbered equations, are unchanged. The added experiments introduce no new formal definitions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: an open-data volumetric transformer, complementary self-supervised and vision-language pretraining, and transfer across classification, segmentation, and retrieval. The additional evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v1 qualitatively notes small-lesion failures; v2 develops an evidence-based interpretation involving decoder choice and training budget. C.3 adds explanations of corruption sensitivity, attributes weak MedSigLIP retrieval partly to text truncation, and interprets longer-report advantages while acknowledging possible confounding by healthy subjects. These substantially expand the discussion of mechanisms and applicability limits.

D1.justification: C.2.3 changes the nnU-Net integration from a promised release upon acceptance to a stated public repository with an explicit address. C.3.1 newly discloses fixed retrieval spacing of 0.5 × 0.5 × 1.0 mm. The pretraining hyperparameters, model specifications, and hardware disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds the MedGemma Technical Report citation in connection with MedSigLIP and discusses additional segmentation comparisons, including SAM-Med3D. The main related-work survey and SPECTRE's claimed relationship to prior transformer and CT foundation models remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: There are localized wording and cross-reference edits, revised acknowledgments, two additional segmentation subsections, and separate CT-RATE and MERLIN retrieval subsections. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained; the added scientific content does not constitute extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: The supplement adds result Tables 9–10 and the dropout plot in Figure 8, while expanding and numbering the dataset table as Table 7. Table 1 loses its AMOS column, although its caption still says four datasets. Existing figure content is retained with resizing and placement changes, including relocation of the UMAP plot.

improvement.justification: v1 included AMOS in quantitative evaluation despite using it for pretraining and discussed small-lesion failures mainly qualitatively. v2 removes that overlapping quantitative comparison and directly measures decoder, training-budget, and tiny-lesion effects, addressing important validity and diagnostic gaps. Broader anatomical and retrieval robustness evidence further strengthens the evaluation. AMOS illustrations and reporting gaps remain, including unexplained Figure 8 bands, but the gains in empirical credibility and characterization of failure conditions are substantial.
